blocks.text: A pressure-vessel weld passes inspection on Friday and by Monday a fine crack has opened along the edge of the weld, with no load applied. Nothing broke the steel; three ordinary ingredients came together while it cooled: hydrogen, a hard microstructure and tensile stress. Control any one of them and the crack does not form.

blocks.markdown: **Hydrogen-induced cold cracking** (also called hydrogen cracking or delayed cracking) occurs in the heat-affected zone of steel welds at low temperature, typically below about 200 $^\circ$C, often hours or days after welding. It needs three conditions together: (1) dissolved **hydrogen**, picked up from moisture, rust, oil or damp flux and absorbed by the weld pool; (2) a **susceptible microstructure**, hard martensite which is brittle and holds hydrogen; and (3) **tensile stress**, from restraint and residual stress. The steel's tendency to form hard martensite is called **hardenability** and can be estimated from its chemical composition.

blocks.title: Carbon equivalent (IIW formula)
blocks.text: The carbon equivalent is a single number that sums the hardening effect of alloying elements as an equivalent amount of carbon, with composition in weight percent: $\text{CE}=C+\dfrac{Mn}{6}+\dfrac{Cr+Mo+V}{5}+\dfrac{Ni+Cu}{15}$. A higher CE means greater hardenability and higher risk of hydrogen cracking.

blocks.caption: IIW carbon equivalent, element symbols denote weight percent

blocks.title: Carbon equivalent of a structural steel
blocks.prompt: A structural steel contains (wt%) C 0.18, Mn 1.40, Cr 0.10, Mo 0.05, V 0.04, Ni 0.20, Cu 0.15. Calculate the carbon equivalent and judge its weldability.

steps.text: Cr, Mo, V and Ni, Cu terms.

blocks.answer: CE is about 0.47. As a rule of thumb (typical guidance) a CE above roughly 0.45 means preheating and low-hydrogen practice are advisable, especially on thick sections.

rows: Usually no preheat in thin sections
Preheat likely for thick plate, low-hydrogen consumables
Preheat, controlled interpass temperature, possibly post-weld heat treatment
blocks.caption: Indicative guidance only; actual requirements depend on thickness, hydrogen level and restraint

blocks.markdown: **Preheating** warms the joint area before welding (typically 100 to 200 $^\circ$C for many carbon steels, depending on CE and thickness). It lowers the cooling rate through the critical range so less martensite forms and the HAZ is softer and tougher. It also keeps the weld hot for longer so that hydrogen, which diffuses faster in warm steel, can escape from the weld and HAZ before the metal cools to the temperature at which cracking occurs. Finally, a lower temperature gradient between weld and plate reduces the thermal stresses.

blocks.title: Breaking the cracking triangle
blocks.text: Preheat and low heat input are different tools: preheat slows cooling (less martensite, hydrogen escapes); low-hydrogen consumables remove the hydrogen; reduced restraint lowers the stress. Heavier sections need more preheat because they remove heat faster.

blocks.markdown: Residual stress and distortion arise from **restrained thermal contraction**. The weld metal and nearby HAZ are heated far above the rest of the plate and want to expand, but the cold plate resists; the hot region is pushed beyond yield in compression and flattened. On cooling, it tries to contract by $\alpha\Delta T$ but is held by the cold surroundings, so tensile stress develops in the weld, rising until it reaches the yield strength. Balancing compressive stress remains in the plate further out.

blocks.caption: Stress from fully restrained contraction; $E$ elastic modulus (MPa), $\alpha$ thermal expansion coefficient (1/$^\circ$C), $\Delta T$ temperature drop ($^\circ$C)

blocks.title: How little cooling produces yield
blocks.prompt: A carbon steel has $E=200$ GPa, $\alpha=12\times10^{-6}$ per $^\circ$C and yield strength 300 MPa. Find the stress rise per $^\circ$C of fully restrained cooling and the temperature drop that brings the weld to yield.
blocks.answer: Each degree of restrained cooling adds about 2.4 MPa; a drop of only about 125 degrees C takes the weld to yield, so residual tensile stresses near the yield strength are normal.

rows: Allow for it in the part dimensions
More weld metal on one side of the plate than the other
Symmetric joint, double-sided welding, pre-set angle
Jigs, backstep sequence, reduced heat input
blocks.caption: Common welding distortions

blocks.title: Residual stress is not removed by inspection
blocks.text: High tensile residual stress near yield adds to applied loads and lowers fatigue life and fracture margin. Stress relief heat treatment, peening or controlled sequences may be required. Restraint with rigid fixtures lowers distortion but raises residual stress.

points: Carbon equivalent $\text{CE}=C+Mn/6+(Cr+Mo+V)/5+(Ni+Cu)/15$ ranks hardenability; higher CE means higher risk of hydrogen cracking.
Hydrogen cracking needs hydrogen, a hard microstructure and tensile stress together.
Preheating slows cooling, giving softer microstructure and time for hydrogen to escape.
Restrained thermal contraction drives residual tensile stress up to yield in the weld and causes shrinkage and distortion.

questions.stem: Which three conditions must be present together for hydrogen-induced cold cracking in a steel weld?

options.text: Oxygen, high carbon and compressive stress
Dissolved hydrogen, a hard martensitic microstructure and tensile stress
Hydrogen, soft ferrite and zero stress
Nitrogen, sulphur and high temperature

questions.correctOptionText: Dissolved hydrogen, a hard martensitic microstructure and tensile stress

distractorRationale.a: Compressive stress would close, not open, cracks, and oxygen is not the cracking agent.
distractorRationale.c: Ferrite is soft and tough, and cracks need a tensile stress to open them.
distractorRationale.d: Cold cracking occurs at low temperature, below about 200 $^\circ$C.

questions.explanation: Hydrogen embrittles a hard, brittle microstructure such as martensite, and tensile stress then opens cracks. Removing any one of the three, for example by lowering hydrogen or hardness, prevents the problem.

questions.stem: A steel has composition (wt%): C 0.22, Mn 1.05, Cr 0.25, Mo 0.08, V 0.02, Ni 0.40, Cu 0.30. Calculate its IIW carbon equivalent.
questions.explanation: The terms are $Mn/6=0.175$, $(Cr+Mo+V)/5=0.070$ and $(Ni+Cu)/15=0.047$. The sum is $\text{CE}=0.22+0.175+0.070+0.047=0.512$, which is above 0.50 and so indicates a steel that needs careful preheat.

questions.stem: Steel A has C 0.10 and Mn 0.9; steel B has C 0.25 and Mn 1.5 (no other alloying). Which is more susceptible to hydrogen cracking in the heat-affected zone?

options.text: Steel A, with carbon equivalent about 0.25
Both equally, since only carbon matters
Neither, since CE has no link to cracking
Steel B, with carbon equivalent about 0.50

questions.correctOptionText: Steel B, with carbon equivalent about 0.50

distractorRationale.a: Steel A has CE of 0.10 + 0.15 = 0.25, lower than B, so it is less susceptible.
distractorRationale.b: Manganese also contributes to hardenability through its term $Mn/6$.
distractorRationale.c: CE is exactly the measure of hardenability used to judge cracking susceptibility.

questions.explanation: The carbon equivalents are 0.25 for A and 0.50 for B, so B has the greater hardenability and cracking risk. Manganese adds $Mn/6$ to the CE.

questions.stem: Which is the main way that preheating a thick steel joint reduces the risk of cold cracking?

options.text: It slows the cooling rate so less martensite forms and hydrogen can escape
It raises the carbon content of the weld
It removes all residual stress
It increases the hydrogen content of the weld

questions.correctOptionText: It slows the cooling rate so less martensite forms and hydrogen can escape

distractorRationale.c: Stress is lowered but not eliminated by preheating.
distractorRationale.d: Preheating helps drive hydrogen out, not in.

questions.explanation: Slower cooling gives a softer, less hardened HAZ and keeps the joint warm so hydrogen diffuses away before the metal cools to cracking temperature. Preheating also lowers thermal gradients and so reduces stress.

questions.stem: For the same steel and the same welding procedure, why does a thicker plate generally need a higher preheat temperature?

options.text: A thicker plate contains more hydrogen
Thicker plate has a lower carbon equivalent
A thicker plate conducts heat away faster, so cooling is more rapid
Thicker plate expands less

questions.correctOptionText: A thicker plate conducts heat away faster, so cooling is more rapid

distractorRationale.a: Hydrogen content depends on consumables and moisture, not on thickness.
distractorRationale.d: Expansion is not the issue; heat flow is.

questions.explanation: Heat flows into the plate in three dimensions, so the thicker the plate the faster the weld cools. A faster cooling rate favours martensite, so more preheat is needed to compensate.

questions.stem: A weld in steel cools by 80 $^\circ$C while its contraction is fully restrained. Take $E=205$ GPa and $\alpha=12\times10^{-6}$ per $^\circ$C. Calculate the tensile stress developed, in MPa.
questions.explanation: The restrained stress is $\sigma=E\alpha\Delta T=205\,000\times12\times10^{-6}\times80=196.8$ MPa. This is below a typical structural steel yield strength, so the elastic estimate applies.

questions.stem: A steel weld metal of yield strength 250 MPa is fully restrained during cooling. With $E=200$ GPa and $\alpha=11.7\times10^{-6}$ per $^\circ$C, calculate the temperature drop after which the stress reaches yield, in $^\circ$C. State what happens to the stress if cooling continues.
questions.explanation: The stress rate is $E\alpha=200\,000\times11.7\times10^{-6}=2.34$ MPa/$^\circ$C, so yield is reached after $250/2.34=106.8$ $^\circ$C. Beyond this the metal yields in tension and the stress stays near yield, which is why residual stresses in welds are close to the yield strength.

questions.stem: A single-V butt weld between two thick plates leaves the plates tilted towards the weld face. Which distortion is this, and why does it occur?

options.text: Transverse shrinkage only, because the root has no weld metal
Buckling, because the plates are thin
Longitudinal bowing, because the weld is too short
Angular distortion, because more weld metal is at the wide top of the V so it contracts more there

questions.correctOptionText: Angular distortion, because more weld metal is at the wide top of the V so it contracts more there

distractorRationale.a: Transverse shrinkage occurs but does not by itself cause tilting out of the plane.
distractorRationale.b: Buckling occurs in thin plate under compressive stress, not in thick butt joints.
distractorRationale.c: Longitudinal bowing relates to the stress along the weld, not the angle of the plate faces.

questions.explanation: A V-groove contains more weld metal near the top than the root, so contraction is greater at the top surface and rotates the plates. Double-V joints and balanced sequences reduce this.

questions.stem: Explain, with reference to hydrogen, microstructure and stress, why preheating and low-hydrogen consumables reduce the risk of cold cracking in the heat-affected zone of a medium-carbon steel weld.
markingGuide: Cold cracking needs hydrogen, martensite and tensile stress
Preheat slows cooling so less martensite and a softer HAZ
Preheat keeps the joint warm so hydrogen diffuses out
Low-hydrogen consumables reduce hydrogen entering the weld pool
Lower thermal gradients also reduce stress; heavier sections need more preheat
questions.explanation: Preheat acts on the microstructure and hydrogen at once, while low-hydrogen consumables remove the hydrogen source. Together they remove two of the three conditions needed for cracking.

questions.stem: Explain how residual stress and distortion arise when a weld is made on a restrained plate. Include the roles of heating, yielding and cooling, and suggest two ways to reduce distortion and one way to reduce residual stress.
markingGuide: Weld region heats and expands but is restrained by the cold plate so it yields in compression
On cooling, the weld contracts but the surrounding plate resists, creating tensile residual stress near yield
Unrestrained contraction appears as shrinkage and distortion (angular, transverse, longitudinal)
Reduce distortion: balanced welding sequence, symmetric joint, jigs or pre-setting, lower heat input
Reduce residual stress: post-weld heat treatment, peening or lower restraint
questions.explanation: The weld metal is yielded when hot, so on cooling it is too short for its place and is pulled into tension by the surrounding metal. The mismatch appears as distortion if the plate is free and as residual stress if it is restrained.
